lessons.title: Place Value: Tens and Ones
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Understand tens and ones
Read and write numbers to 99
Compare 2-digit numbers
lessons.reading_material:
Numbers bigger than 10 have two parts: TENS and ONES. In the number 35, the 3 is in the tens place (meaning 3 groups of ten = 30) and the 5 is in the ones place (meaning 5 ones). So 35 = 30 + 5. We use a place value chart to organise digits.

Place Value: Tens and Ones is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Understand tens and ones; Read and write numbers to 99; Compare 2-digit numbers. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: tens, ones, place value, digit, 2-digit numbers. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

lessons.title: Reading: Fiction and Non-Fiction
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Distinguish between fiction and non-fiction
Use a contents page and index
Summarise a non-fiction text
lessons.reading_material:
Books can be FICTION (made-up stories) or NON-FICTION (true information). Fiction has characters, settings, plots, and is imagined. Non-fiction books have: CONTENTS PAGE (shows what's in the book and page numbers), INDEX (alphabetical list at the back), HEADINGS, PHOTOGRAPHS/diagrams. A dictionary, encyclopaedia, and science book are non-fiction.

lessons.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Explain the main idea of the seasons.
Give an example of the seasons in everyday life.
Answer questions about the seasons correctly.
lessons.reading_material:
Children learn about the four seasons and how weather and nature change through the year.

Before getting into the details, think about where The Seasons shows up outside of the classroom. Ideas in Science are rarely just for tests -- they usually connect to things you notice in everyday life, and part of getting good at Science is training yourself to spot those connections instead of treating school topics as separate from the rest of the world.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Explain the main idea of the seasons; Give an example of the seasons in everyday life; Answer questions about the seasons correctly. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: Seasons. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Class discussion and worksheet on the seasons; Hands-on activity exploring the seasons. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

For homework, Talk with a family member about what you learned in 'The Seasons' today. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review 'The Seasons' before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

So, in short: The Seasons matters because it connects to bigger ideas coming later in Science. Don't worry if it doesn't feel completely natural on the first read -- that's normal for any new idea. Read it again, try the practice activity, and check yourself against the learning goals above; understanding usually arrives on the second or third pass, not the first.

It's worth pausing to ask why The Seasons is part of the Science curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. The Seasons is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Science start to make a lot more sense.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Science is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. The Seasons is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

To wrap up: The Seasons is one small piece of Science, but it's a piece worth knowing solidly, because later lessons will lean on it without stopping to re-explain it. Take your time with it now, ask questions if anything feels unclear, and come back to reread this lesson whenever a later topic reminds you of it -- that kind of revisiting is exactly how real understanding builds up over a school year.

lessons.title: Continents and Oceans
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Name the 7 continents
Name the 5 oceans
lessons.reading_material:
Earth has 7 continents: Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia/Oceania, Antarctica. The 5 oceans are Pacific (largest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic. Continents are large landmasses; oceans are huge bodies of salt water.

Before getting into the details, think about where Continents and Oceans shows up outside of the classroom. Ideas in Geography are rarely just for tests -- they usually connect to things you notice in everyday life, and part of getting good at Geography is training yourself to spot those connections instead of treating school topics as separate from the rest of the world.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Name the 7 continents; Name the 5 oceans. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: continent, ocean, landmass, Africa, Asia, Pacific. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Label a world map with continents and oceans; Sort country cards to their continents. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

For homework, Colour and label a world map with continents. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review this lesson before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

So, in short: Continents and Oceans matters because it connects to bigger ideas coming later in Geography. Don't worry if it doesn't feel completely natural on the first read -- that's normal for any new idea. Read it again, try the practice activity, and check yourself against the learning goals above; understanding usually arrives on the second or third pass, not the first.

It's worth pausing to ask why Continents and Oceans is part of the Geography curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. Continents and Oceans is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Geography start to make a lot more sense.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Geography is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. Continents and Oceans is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

To wrap up: Continents and Oceans is one small piece of Geography, but it's a piece worth knowing solidly, because later lessons will lean on it without stopping to re-explain it. Take your time with it now, ask questions if anything feels unclear, and come back to reread this lesson whenever a later topic reminds you of it -- that kind of revisiting is exactly how real understanding builds up over a school year.

lessons.title: Weather and Climate
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Distinguish weather from climate
Describe different climate zones
lessons.reading_material:
Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere (sunny, rainy, windy). Climate is the average weather over many years for a region. Tropical climates near the equator are hot and wet. Polar climates near the poles are cold. Temperate climates have four seasons.

It's worth pausing to ask why Weather and Climate is part of the Geography curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. Weather and Climate is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Geography start to make a lot more sense.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to do a few specific things: Distinguish weather from climate; Describe different climate zones. Keep these goals in mind as you read -- they're not just a checklist for the teacher, they're a way for you to test yourself afterwards and see whether the lesson has really sunk in.

The key words to know for this lesson are: weather, climate, equator, tropics, polar, temperate. New topics often come with new vocabulary, and in Geography the vocabulary usually isn't just decoration -- each of these words points to a specific idea that you'll need again in later lessons, so it's worth being able to explain each one in your own words, not just recognise it when you see it.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

A good way to practise this lesson is: Keep a weather diary for one week; Match climate zones to regions on a world map. Doing something hands-on with an idea -- rather than only reading about it -- is one of the fastest ways to make it stick, because your brain remembers things you've actually done far better than things you've only read.

lessons.title: Ancient Civilisations Overview
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Name ancient civilisations
Identify their locations on a map
lessons.reading_material:
Long ago, people built great civilisations. Ancient Egypt had pharaohs and pyramids. Mesopotamia (modern Iraq) had the first writing. Ancient China built the Great Wall. Ancient Greece created democracy and the Olympics. Ancient Rome built an empire across Europe.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning World History is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. Ancient Civilisations Overview is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Name ancient civilisations; Identify their locations on a map. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: civilisation, ancient, pharaoh, pyramid, empire, democracy. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Match civilisation to location on world map; Draw or model a pyramid. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

For homework, Draw one symbol from an ancient civilisation and explain its meaning. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review this lesson before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

So, in short: Ancient Civilisations Overview matters because it connects to bigger ideas coming later in World History. Don't worry if it doesn't feel completely natural on the first read -- that's normal for any new idea. Read it again, try the practice activity, and check yourself against the learning goals above; understanding usually arrives on the second or third pass, not the first.

Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. Before getting into the details, think about where Ancient Civilisations Overview shows up outside of the classroom. Ideas in World History are rarely just for tests -- they usually connect to things you notice in everyday life, and part of getting good at World History is training yourself to spot those connections instead of treating school topics as separate from the rest of the world.

lessons.title: The Five Pillars of Islam
lessons.subject: Islamic Studies
learning_objectives: Name and describe the Five Pillars
Explain why each pillar is important
Reflect on how the pillars guide daily life
lessons.reading_material:
The Five Pillars are the core acts of worship in Islam: Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (5 daily prayers), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah). They are the foundation of a Muslim's life.

It's worth pausing to ask why The Five Pillars of Islam is part of the Islamic Studies curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. The Five Pillars of Islam is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Islamic Studies start to make a lot more sense.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Name and describe the Five Pillars; Explain why each pillar is important; Reflect on how the pillars guide daily life. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj, prayer. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Create a Five Pillars booklet; Discuss: how does each pillar help the community?. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review this lesson before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

So, in short: The Five Pillars of Islam matters because it connects to bigger ideas coming later in Islamic Studies. Don't worry if it doesn't feel completely natural on the first read -- that's normal for any new idea. Read it again, try the practice activity, and check yourself against the learning goals above; understanding usually arrives on the second or third pass, not the first.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Islamic Studies is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. The Five Pillars of Islam is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Before getting into the details, think about where The Five Pillars of Islam shows up outside of the classroom. Ideas in Islamic Studies are rarely just for tests -- they usually connect to things you notice in everyday life, and part of getting good at Islamic Studies is training yourself to spot those connections instead of treating school topics as separate from the rest of the world.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

To wrap up: The Five Pillars of Islam is one small piece of Islamic Studies, but it's a piece worth knowing solidly, because later lessons will lean on it without stopping to re-explain it. Take your time with it now, ask questions if anything feels unclear, and come back to reread this lesson whenever a later topic reminds you of it -- that kind of revisiting is exactly how real understanding builds up over a school year.

learning_objectives: Distinguish myths from legends
Retell a Greek or Norse myth
Explain why cultures created myths
lessons.reading_material:
Myths are ancient stories used to explain the world — why the sun rises, how fire was created, where the seasons come from. Greek myths: Prometheus stole fire for humans. Persephone explains why we have winter. Norse myths: Odin, Thor, and Loki are gods in Viking stories. Legends are stories about real (or partly real) heroes that have grown over time: King Arthur in Britain, Robin Hood, Sundiata Keita of Mali. Both myths and legends reveal what a culture values.

info_cards.fact: "Wanderer above the Sea of Fog" by Caspar David Friedrich. A German Romantic painting of a man looking out over a sea of clouds from a mountain.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Arnolfini Portrait
info_cards.fact: "The Arnolfini Portrait" by Jan van Eyck. An early Northern Renaissance painting of a merchant and his wife in a Flemish home.

info_cards.fact: "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte" by Georges Seurat. A pointillist painting made entirely of tiny dots of paint.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Kiss
info_cards.fact: "The Kiss" by Gustav Klimt. An Austrian painting decorated with gold leaf showing two figures embracing.

info_cards.fact: "Bal du moulin de la Galette" by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. An Impressionist painting of dancers and diners in a Paris garden.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Luncheon of the Boating Party
info_cards.fact: "Luncheon of the Boating Party" by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Shows friends relaxing on a balcony overlooking the Seine river in France.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Impression, Sunrise
info_cards.fact: "Impression, Sunrise" by Claude Monet. The painting that gave the Impressionist movement its name.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Garden of Earthly Delights
info_cards.fact: "The Garden of Earthly Delights" by Hieronymus Bosch. A detailed triptych painting full of imaginative creatures and landscapes.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The School of Athens
info_cards.fact: "The School of Athens" by Raphael. A Renaissance fresco showing famous Greek philosophers like Plato and Aristotle together.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Motherland Calls
info_cards.fact: "The Motherland Calls" by Yevgeny Vuchetich. One of the tallest statues in the world, located in Volgograd, Russia, honouring wartime resilience.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Spring Temple Buddha
info_cards.fact: "Spring Temple Buddha" by Modern Chinese sculptors. One of the tallest statues in the world, located in Henan, China.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Ushiku Daibutsu
info_cards.fact: "Ushiku Daibutsu" by Modern Japanese sculptors. A huge bronze Buddha statue in Ibaraki, Japan.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Leshan Giant Buddha
info_cards.fact: "Leshan Giant Buddha" by Tang dynasty sculptors. An enormous stone Buddha statue carved into a cliff in Sichuan, China.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Angel of the North
info_cards.fact: "The Angel of the North" by Antony Gormley. A huge steel sculpture of an angel standing beside a motorway in England.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Cloud Gate (The Bean)
info_cards.fact: "Cloud Gate (The Bean)" by Anish Kapoor. A giant, mirror-like stainless steel sculpture in Chicago's Millennium Park.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Balloon Dog
info_cards.fact: "Balloon Dog" by Jeff Koons. A large, brightly coloured stainless-steel sculpture shaped like a balloon animal.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Charging Bull
info_cards.fact: "The Charging Bull" by Arturo Di Modica. A bronze bull statue near Wall Street in New York City, symbolizing financial optimism.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Atlas (Rockefeller Center)
info_cards.fact: "Atlas (Rockefeller Center)" by Lee Lawrie. A large bronze statue of the Greek titan Atlas holding up the heavens, in New York City.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Christ of the Abyss
info_cards.fact: "Christ of the Abyss" by Guido Galletti. An underwater bronze statue of Christ placed in the Mediterranean Sea off Italy.

info_cards.title: Did You Know?
info_cards.fact: Octopuses have three hearts.

info_cards.title: Did You Know?
info_cards.fact: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.

info_cards.title: Famous Places
info_cards.fact: The Great Wall of China is so long that it stretches for thousands of miles.

info_cards.title: Philosophical Quote
info_cards.fact: "Know thyself." — inscribed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, a saying attributed to ancient Greek philosophy.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "The only way to do great work is to love what you do." — Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Leonardo da Vinci
info_cards.fact: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian artist and inventor who painted the Mona Lisa and filled notebooks with designs for flying machines centuries before airplanes existed.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: A Brief History of Time
info_cards.fact: "A Brief History of Time" by physicist Stephen Hawking (1988) explains big ideas about the universe — like black holes and the Big Bang — in everyday language.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: The Story of My Life
info_cards.fact: "The Story of My Life" by Helen Keller is the memoir of how Helen Keller, who was deaf and blind from infancy, learned to read, write, and communicate.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Marie Curie
info_cards.fact: "Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood." — Polish-French physicist and chemist who discovered the elements polonium and radium and won two Nobel Prizes.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Albert Einstein
info_cards.fact: "Imagination is more important than knowledge." — German-born physicist who developed the theory of relativity and won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Leonardo da Vinci
info_cards.fact: "Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication." — Italian Renaissance painter, engineer, and scientist who painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
info_cards.fact: "Neither a lofty degree of intelligence nor imagination... is essential to genius. Love, love, love, that is the soul of genius." — Austrian composer who wrote over 600 works and is considered one of the greatest composers in Western music history.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ludwig van Beethoven
info_cards.fact: "Music can change the world." — German composer who continued composing symphonies even after losing his hearing.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Galileo Galilei
info_cards.fact: "I have never met a man so ignorant that I couldn't learn something from him." — Italian astronomer and physicist who improved the telescope and supported the idea that Earth orbits the Sun.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Isaac Newton
info_cards.fact: "If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants." — English physicist and mathematician who described the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Charles Darwin
info_cards.fact: "It is not the strongest of the species that survives, but the most adaptable." — English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection was published in On the Origin of Species.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Alexander Graham Bell
info_cards.fact: "Before anything else, preparation is the key to success." — Scottish-born inventor credited with patenting the first practical telephone.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Thomas Edison
info_cards.fact: "I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work." — American inventor credited with developing the practical electric light bulb and the phonograph.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Nikola Tesla
info_cards.fact: "The present is theirs; the future, for which I really worked, is mine." — Serbian-American inventor and engineer who pioneered alternating-current (AC) electrical systems.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Rosalind Franklin
info_cards.fact: "Science and everyday life cannot and should not be separated." — British chemist whose X-ray images were crucial to discovering the structure of DNA.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Katherine Johnson
info_cards.fact: "Like any survivor, I'm grateful to have been knocked down... It only made me work harder." — American mathematician whose calculations were vital to NASA's early human spaceflight missions.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: George Washington Carver
info_cards.fact: "Education is the key to unlock the golden door of freedom." — American agricultural scientist who developed hundreds of new uses for the peanut and other crops.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Frederick Douglass
info_cards.fact: "Once you learn to read, you will be forever free." — American social reformer who escaped slavery and became a leading abolitionist writer and speaker.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Harriet Tubman
info_cards.fact: "Every great dream begins with a dreamer." — American abolitionist who escaped slavery and led dozens of others to freedom via the Underground Railroad.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Sojourner Truth
info_cards.fact: "Truth is powerful and it prevails." — American abolitionist and women's rights activist born into slavery, known for her speech 'Ain't I a Woman?'

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Booker T. Washington
info_cards.fact: "Success is to be measured not so much by the position one has reached in life as by the obstacles overcome." — American educator who founded the Tuskegee Institute to provide education for African Americans.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Susan B. Anthony
info_cards.fact: "Failure is impossible." — American activist who fought for women's right to vote and helped found the National Woman Suffrage Association.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
info_cards.fact: "The moment we begin to fear the opinions of others... we have begun to die." — American women's rights leader who co-organized the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention.

lessons.title: Countries and Flags
lessons.subject: General Knowledge
learning_objectives: Identify 10 countries and their flags
Locate them on a map
Know their capital cities
lessons.reading_material:
Every country has a flag — a special symbol that represents it. The United Kingdom has the Union Jack. The USA has 50 stars for its states. Japan's flag shows a red circle (the rising sun). Capital cities are the official centres of government. London is the capital of the UK; Washington D.C. is the capital of the USA; Tokyo is the capital of Japan.

Before getting into the details, think about where Countries and Flags shows up outside of the classroom. lessons.reading_material:
Arabic is spoken by over 300 million people and is one of the official languages of the United Nations. In Arabic, we say 'مرحبا' (Marhaba) for hello and 'مع السلامة' (Ma'a as-salama) for goodbye. Numbers: واحد، اثنان، ثلاثة، أربعة، خمسة، ستة، سبعة، ثمانية، تسعة، عشرة (1–10). Arabic is written right to left.
